text: UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA CFO RICK INC, Case No. 25-cv-09896-EMC Plaintiff, ORDER DENYING PLAINTIFF’S v. MOTION FOR ATTORNEY’S FEES MICHAEL YOUNG, Docket No. 55 Defendant. This is one of two “CFO Rick” cases. Defendant Michael Young is the managing and majority member of an LLC known as Millwright Holdings (“Millwright”). The minority member Plaintiff Rick Belgarde. In addition to being the minority member of Millwright, Mr. Belgarde was Millwright’s CFO, and his separately-owned company, CFO Rick, provided financial and accounting services to Millwright. At some point, the relationship between Mr. Young and Mr. Belgarde soured, and Mr. Young accused Mr. Belgarde and CFO Rick of engaging in misconduct vis-à-vis Millwright. Mr. Young thus initiated an arbitration against both Mr. Belgarde and CFO Rick. CFO Rick filed the instant case, largely seeking a declaration that it could not be compelled to arbitration. The Court agreed with CFO Rick, but the case did not wrap up immediately thereafter because Mr. Young brought counterclaims (on his behalf and on behalf of Millwright). CFO Rick moved to dismiss the counterclaims, and the Court granted the motion after Mr. Young failed to oppose. A final judgment has now been entered, and the only matter left to resolve is a motion for attorney’s fees filed by CFO Rick. The main reason why CFO Rick seeks fees is because Mr. to dismiss. See Mot. at 3 (emphasizing that fees are not being sought just because Mr. Young filed counterclaims; fees are sought because the “counterclaims were maintained after a written demand for their withdrawal that identified their specific defects . . . and offered a costless exit through dismissal without prejudice, and because, after refusing that demand, Defendant and his counsel then did nothing to prosecute or defend that [counter]claims”) (emphasis added). CFO Rick asks for fees pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1927 and the Court’s inherent authority. Having considered the parties’ briefs and accompanying submissions, as well as the oral argument of counsel, the Court hereby DENIES the motion for fees. I. FACTUAL & PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND As noted above, CFO Rick filed this lawsuit, seeking a declaration that it could not be compelled to arbitration. Mr. Young moved to dismiss the case and also to compel arbitration. On February 17, 2026, the Court ruled against Mr. Young and directed the parties to meet and confer to determine whether they can reach a

The response was due on March 27, 2026. See Fed. R. Civ. Rubinstein Decl. ¶ 5 (emphasis added). In short, CFO Rick gave Mr. Young three days to withdraw his counterclaims, notwithstanding the fact that CFO Rick’s response to the counterclaims was not due until some four weeks later. Mr. Young did not respond by CFO Rick’s deadline of April 2, 2026. See Rubinstein Decl. ¶ 6. Approximately a week later, CFO Rick filed its motion to dismiss on April 8, 2026. The parties agreed that Mr. Young could have an extension to file his opposition to the motion to dismiss. After Mr. Young failed to file an opposition by the extended deadline, see Docket No. 48 (order setting extended deadline of May 14, 2026), CFO Rick filed a statement noting the failure to oppose. See Docket No. 49 (statement filed on May 16, 2026). The Court then issued an order to show cause, warning Mr. Young that a failure to respond to the order to show cause could lead to a granting of the motion to dismiss. See Docket No. 50 (order). Mr. Young did not file a response to the order to show cause, and so, the Court dismissed the counterclaims. See Docket No. 51 (order filed on May 21, 2026). In its order, the Court noted: The state court action was filed in San Francisco Superior Court. See CFO Rick Inc. v. Millwright Holdings LLC, No. CGC-26634912. The Court takes judicial notice that CFO Rick The dismissal is with prejudice to the extent that the Court shall not permit Mr. Young to pursue the counterclaims in this forum. However, to be clear, the Court has not adjudicated the merits of Mr. Young’s counterclaims. The Court expresses no opinion as to whether Mr. Young may pursue his counterclaims in another forum. Docket No. 51 (Order at 2). Now that the entire case has been disposed of, CFO Rick asks to be awarded three categories of attorneys’ fees: (1) fees related to CFO Rick’s motion to extend time to respond to Mr. Young’s counterclaims ($4,761, representing 9 hours of attorney time), see Mot. at 9; (2) fees related to CFO Rick’s motion to dismiss Mr. Young’s counterclaims ($17,215, representing 31.3 hours of attorney time), see Mot. at 8; and (3) fees related to the pending fee motion ($6,545, representing 11.9 hours of attorney time).2 See Reply at 15. II. DISCUSSION A. Legal Standard CFO Rick argues that attorneys’ fees should be awarded pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1927 or the Court’s inherent authority.3 1. Section 1927 Section 1927 states: Any attorney or other person admitted to conduct cases in any court of the United States . . . who so multiplies the proceedings in any case unreasonably and vexatiously may be required by the court to satisfy personally the excess costs, expenses, and attorneys’ fees reasonably incurred because of such conduct. 28 U.S.C. § 1927 (emphasis added). According to CFO Rick, it is not seeking fees for all of the work its attorneys did. See, e.g., Reply at 13 (arguing that the fee “request was build conservatively” as it “excludes the time spent preparing the March 30 demand letter itself, excludes entries in which motion work was block- billed with other tasks, and reproduces the time entries verbatim from the firm’s invoices”). In his opposition, Mr. Young points out that CFO Rick has not moved for fees pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 – nor could it because it never followed the safe harbor procedures (although arguably its demand letter accomplished much of the same purpose). In Only an attorney may be sanctioned under § 1927 (not, e.g., the client or a law firm). See Kaass Law v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 799 F.3d 1290, 1293 (9th

metadata.case_name: CFO Rick Inc v. Young

text: because it never followed the safe harbor procedures (although arguably its demand letter accomplished much of the same purpose). In Only an attorney may be sanctioned under § 1927 (not, e.g., the client or a law firm). See Kaass Law v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 799 F.3d 1290, 1293 (9th Cir. 2015). And as indicated by the bolded language above, § 1927 requires that an attorney’s “conduct ‘multipl[ied] the proceedings’ beyond what would have occurred otherwise. This occurs when misconduct delays or extends litigation, requiring additional effort or expense that would not have been necessary.” Weissman v. Cheokas, No. 23-12527, 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 17719, at *18 (11th Cir. June 18, 2026). In addition to the above, “[t]he imposition of sanctions under [the statute] requires a finding of bad faith, which is assessed under a subjective standard.” Pacific Harbor Cap., Inc. v. Carnival Air Lines, Inc., 210 F.3d 1112, 1118 (9th Cir. 2000) (internal quotation marks omitted). "Bad faith is present when an attorney knowingly or recklessly raises a frivolous argument, or argues a meritorious claim for the purpose of harassing an opponent." In re Keegan Mgmt. Co., Sec. Litig., 78 F.3d 431, 436 (9th Cir. 1996). In general, “bad judgment[] or well-intentioned zeal” is not bad faith. Grider v. Keystone Health Plan Cent., Inc., 580 F.3d 119, 142 (3d Cir. 2009); see also B.K.B. v. Maui Police Dep’t, 276 F.3d 1091, 1107 (9th Cir. 2002) (“‘Reckless nonfrivolous filings, without more, may not be sanctioned.’”); Crossfirst Bank v. Vieste Spe LLC, No. CV-18-01637-PHX-DLR, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 121279, at *8 (D. Ariz. June 2, 2026) (“The claims Plaintiffs brought, though ultimately unsuccessful, were not so lacking in legal or factual foundation as to permit an inference that counsel pursued them for purposes of unreasonably and vexatiously multiplying court proceedings rather than to vindicate their clients' asserted rights.”). “Fees on fees” may be assessed under § 1927. See Blixseth v. Yellowstone Mt. Club, LLC, 854 F.3d 626, 631 (9th Cir. 2017) (“[W]e conclude that the costs of obtaining sanctions may be included in a sanctions under § 1927.”). 2. Court’s Inherent Authority “[S]anctions imposed under the district court's inherent authority require a bad faith finding.” Lahiri v. Universal Music & Video Distrib. Corp., 606 F.3d 1216, 1219 (9th Cir. 2010). “[M]ere recklessness, without more, does not justify sanctions under a court’s inherent power,” combined with an additional factor such as frivolousness,

metadata.case_name: CFO Rick Inc v. Young

text: Authority “[S]anctions imposed under the district court's inherent authority require a bad faith finding.” Lahiri v. Universal Music & Video Distrib. Corp., 606 F.3d 1216, 1219 (9th Cir. 2010). “[M]ere recklessness, without more, does not justify sanctions under a court’s inherent power,” combined with an additional factor such as frivolousness, harassment, or an improper purpose.” Fink v. Gomez, 239 F.3d 989, 933-94 (9th Cir. 2001). “[A] finding of bad faith does not require that the legal and factual basis for the action prove totally frivolous; where a litigant is substantially motivated by vindictiveness, obduracy, or mala fides, the assertion of a colorable claim will not bar the assessment of attorney's fees.” Id. at 992. Sanctions under a court’s inherent authority are “compensatory rather than punitive in nature. In other words, the fee award may go no further than to redress the wronged party ‘for losses sustained.’” Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Haeger, 581 U.S. 101, 108 (2017). “That means, pretty much by definition, that the court can shift only those attorney’s fees incurred because of the misconduct at issue.” Id. B. Fees Related to CFO Rick’s Motion to Extend Time CFO Rick asks first for fees for the time its attorney spent on CFO Rick’s motion to extend time to respond to Mr. Young’s counterclaims. According to CFO Rick, its attorney spent 9 hours on the matter, totaling $4,761. The request for fees is denied. For purposes of § 1927, CFO Rick has failed to show that Mr. Young’s attorney vexatiously and unreasonably multiplied proceedings. CFO Rick gave Mr. Young’s attorney only one day (technically, a little less than one day) to respond to its request for an extension of time. CFO Rick could easily have given Mr. Young and his attorney more than just one day, especially because its response to Mr. Young’s counterclaims was not due for more than a week later. Notably, the same day that the Court directed the parties to meet and confer on the issue of an extension (the Court’s order issued just one day after CFO Rick filed its motion to extend), Mr. Young and his attorney promptly agreed to an extension. The same facts above also establish that Mr. Young and/or his attorney did not act in bad faith and therefore fees are not warranted, whether under § 1927 or pursuant to the Court’s inherent authority.4 C. Fees Related to CFO

text: Mr. Young and his attorney promptly agreed to an extension. The same facts above also establish that Mr. Young and/or his attorney did not act in bad faith and therefore fees are not warranted, whether under § 1927 or pursuant to the Court’s inherent authority.4 C. Fees Related to CFO Rick’s Motion to Dismiss Counterclaims CFO Rick next seeks the attorneys’ fees it incurred for filing its motion to dismiss Mr. Young’s counterclaims. This request for fees – totaling more than $17,000 – is also denied. CFO Rick has not made a sufficient showing of bad faith which is needed for fees to be awarded under § 1927 or pursuant to the Court’s inherent authority. There are two reasons why there is an inadequate showing of bad faith. First, CFO Rick gave Mr. Young only three days after its demand letter (of March 30, 2026) to withdraw his counterclaims. Similar to above, this compressed timeline was not justified, especially given that CFO Rick’s response to the counterclaims was not due until several weeks later. Furthermore, CFO Rick’s demand letter raised several issues: e.g., whether Mr. Young lacked standing to pursue claims on behalf of Millwright, whether the federal trade secret misappropriation claim was viable, and whether there was supplemental jurisdiction if the federal claim were dismissed). For Mr. Young and his attorney to vet the issues would require more than just three days, particularly as CFO Rick’s arguments for dismissal, as presented in its demand letter, were not obviously meritorious.5 See In re Girardi, 611 F.3d 1027, 1064 (9th Cir. 2010) (noting that a party has a duty under § 1927 “to correct or withdraw litigation positions after it becomes obvious that they are meritless”) (emphasis added); Schmitzer v. County of Riverside, 26 Fed. Appx. 701, 703 (9th Cir. 2002) (rejecting defendant’s contention that plaintiff’s “claims were so meritless that the summary judgment process alone constituted an unnecessary multiplication of the proceedings”) (emphasis added); Am. Honda Motor Co. v. Motorcycle Info. Network, Inc., No. 5:04-cv-12-Oc-10GRJ, 2007 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 97949, at *19-20 (M.D. Fla. Sept. 17, 2007) For instance, if Mr. Young’s counterclaims were deemed compulsory in nature, then there would be supplemental jurisdiction over those counterclaims. See Oneida Indian Nation v. Phillips, 981 F.3d 157, 170 n.62 (2d Cir. 2020) (“Phillips's counterclaim, which seeks relief mirroring that sought by the Nation, thus arises out of a common nucleus of

metadata.case_name: CFO Rick Inc v. Young

text: Mr. Young’s counterclaims were deemed compulsory in nature, then there would be supplemental jurisdiction over those counterclaims. See Oneida Indian Nation v. Phillips, 981 F.3d 157, 170 n.62 (2d Cir. 2020) (“Phillips's counterclaim, which seeks relief mirroring that sought by the Nation, thus arises out of a common nucleus of operative fact, falling squarely within our supplemental jurisdiction.”); Martin v. Law Offices of John F. Edwards, 262 F.R.D. 534, 536 (S.D. Cal. 2009) (“Permissive counterclaims encompass ‘any claim that is not compulsory’ or does not ‘arise out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the (noting that “[t]he Eleventh Circuit has recognized that an award of sanctions under §1927 is appropriate when an attorney fails to abandon a claim and instead goes forward knowing that the evidence will not support the claim” – e.g., the appellate court previously held that a “trial court properly sanctioned an attorney who failed to abandon a case when discovery made it clear that there were no viable claims alleged in the complaint”) (emphasis added). Second, Mr. Young had a fair reason not to withdraw his counterclaims as demanded by CFO Rick. As the parties had previously discussed in their meet-and-confers, Mr. Young was concerned that, if he withdrew the counterclaims, that would constitute a forfeiture of the counterclaims if those claims were deemed compulsory in nature. Although CFO Rick had agreed to a dismissal “without prejudice” of the counterclaims, that was not a clear agreement that CFO Rick would be willing to give up the argument of forfeiture of compulsory counterclaims. At the hearing on the fee motion, CFO Rick suggested that, if that was really Mr. Young’s concern, he still could – and should – have withdrawn his counterclaims because, before CFO Rick even issued its demand letter of March 30, 2026, it had filed suit against Mr. Young and Millwright in state court and served them with the summons and complaint. In other words, there was a forum where Mr. Young and Millwright could assert their counterclaims; this forum was no longer necessary. But it was not unreasonable for Mr. Young and Millwright to first ensure that their counterclaims (or rather, as referred to in state court, the cross-complaint) could be filed and then docketed by the state court. Given that their conduct in not immediately dismissing the counterclaims herein was not unreasonable, Mr. Young cannot be said

metadata.case_name: CFO Rick Inc v. Young

text: for Mr. Young and Millwright to first ensure that their counterclaims (or rather, as referred to in state court, the cross-complaint) could be filed and then docketed by the state court. Given that their conduct in not immediately dismissing the counterclaims herein was not unreasonable, Mr. Young cannot be said to have acted in bad faith. The Court did, at the hearing, have some concern as to why Mr. Young did not tell CFO Rick that he was not going to oppose the motion to dismiss once the cross-complaint was actually on file in state court. But as it turns out, Mr. Young’s answer and Millwright’s answer and cross- complaint were initially rejected by the clerk of the state court (on or about April 24, 2026), which then led CFO Rick to seek entry of default, when then led Mr. Young and Millwright to move to set aside the default so that they could answer and/or file the cross-complaint. The state court did not grant Mr. Young and Millwright relief until August 5, 2026.6 Given the above, there is at least a fair argument that Mr. Young (and Millwright) did not act unreasonably and in bad faith. Mr. Young had a reason why he did not reach out to CFO Rick about not opposing the motion to dismiss the counterclaims; the cross-complaint in state court was still up in the air. At the same time, he had a reason not to substantively oppose the motion to dismiss – i.e., he believed that the state court was the forum to litigate the counterclaims/cross- complaint. To be sure, there is room to argue that the better practice would have been for Mr. Young to reach out to CFO Rick on the motion to dismiss instead of simply staying silent. But given the earlier stalemate where the parties could not agree on a dismissal of the counterclaims and the already bitter litigation in state court, Mr. Young’s actions or omissions were not so unreasonable as to constitute bad faith.7 D. “Fees on Fees” Because the Court has concluded above that fees should not be awarded to CFO Rick, its request for “fees on fees” is also denied. E. Mr. Young’s Fee Request In his opposition brief, Mr. Young states that he is also moving for fees: “Mr. Young is separately moving under Civil Local Rule 7-8 and 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for the

metadata.case_name: CFO Rick Inc v. Young

text: be awarded to CFO Rick, its request for “fees on fees” is also denied. E. Mr. Young’s Fee Request In his opposition brief, Mr. Young states that he is also moving for fees: “Mr. Young is separately moving under Civil Local Rule 7-8 and 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for the fees incurred in opposing this motion.” Opp’n at 14. The Court denies this request for procedural and substantive reasons. First, as a procedural matter, Mr. Young cannot make an affirmative motion in his opposition brief. Second, as a substantive matter, even though the Court is denying CFO Rick’s fee motion, it is not entirely meritless. Quite frankly, if both parties had worked more cooperatively and reasonably, then neither one would have had to incur fees. / / / / / / The Court takes judicial notice of the state court filings. As above, even if the Court were inclined to grant fees, the amount sought by CFO Rick is excessive. As one example, the billing records submitted by CFO Rick show that, on March 29, Til. CONCLUSION For the reasons stated above, CFO Rick’s motion for attorney’s fees is denied. This order disposes of Docket No. 55. IT IS SO ORDERED. || Dated: August 23, 2026 EDWA . text: UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA JOSEPH P. HART, Case No. 25-cv-04501-RFL Plaintiff, ORDER GRANTING IN PART AND v. DENYING IN PART MOTION TO DISMISS COUNTY OF MENDOCINO, et al., Re: Dkt. No. 44 Defendants. On April 13, 2026, the Court granted in part and denied in part Defendants’ motion to dismiss Plaintiff Joseph Hart’s amended complaint. (Dkt. No. 40.) The Court found that the complaint stated claims for deliberate indifference to Hart’s medical needs, cruel and unusual punishment, and negligence against Defendant Eldon Johnston based on his denial of Hart’s prescription medication in 2024, and a claim for First Amendment retaliation against Johnston. (Id. at 13.)1 The Court granted the motion to dismiss Hart’s remaining claims with leave to amend. (Id. at 13–14.) Hart filed a second amended complaint, asserting eleven claims: (1) violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act (“ADA”), (2) deliberate indifference to medical needs in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment, (3) unconstitutional conditions of confinement and punitive solitary placement in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment, (4) violation of procedural due process under the Fourteenth Amendment, (5) retaliation under the First Amendment, (6) Monell liability, (7) negligence, (8) medical negligence, (9) violation of the Bane Act, (10) intentional infliction of emotional distress (“IIED”), and (11) violation of All references to page numbers for filings on the docket refer to ECF pagination. California Government Code section 845.6. (Dkt. No. 43 (“SAC”).) Defendants move to dismiss all claims except for the First Amendment retaliation claim. (See Dkt. No. 44.) For the reasons that follow, the motion to dismiss is GRANTED IN PART AND DENIED IN PART. This order assumes the reader’s familiarity with the facts of this case, the applicable legal standard, and both sides’ arguments. Bane Act, IIED, and Section 845.6 Claims (Claims 9, 10, 11). The motion to dismiss these claims is granted. These claims were not included in the first amended complaint. The Court’s prior order informed Hart that he “may not add new claims . . . without leave of the Court or stipulation by the parties pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15.” (Dkt. No. 40 at 14.) Hart did not receive leave from the Court to add these claims, nor did he file a stipulation permitting him to add these claims pursuant to Rule 15. Accordingly, the addition of these claims exceeds the scope of the Court’s order granting leave

metadata.case_name: Hart v. County of Mendocino

text: Procedure 15.” (Dkt. No. 40 at 14.) Hart did not receive leave from the Court to add these claims, nor did he file a stipulation permitting him to add these claims pursuant to Rule 15. Accordingly, the addition of these claims exceeds the scope of the Court’s order granting leave to amend, and the claims are dismissed. See Strifling v. Twitter Inc., No. 22-cv-07739-JST, 2024 WL 54976, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 4, 2024). Dismissal is without prejudice to Hart seeking leave to add these claims pursuant to Rule 15 or a stipulation. ADA Claim (Claim 1). The second amended complaint fails to state an ADA claim. To the extent that this claim is based on Defendants’ allegedly withholding medical treatment, the claim fails because “the ADA does not create a federal cause of action for prisoners challenging the medical treatment provided for their underlying disabilities.” Alapati v. City & Cnty. of San Francisco, No. 21-cv-04144-SI, 2022 WL 991724, at *12 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 1, 2022) (cleaned up). Hart also alleges that Defendants discriminated against him under a failure-to- accommodate theory. He alleges that the County “failed to make reasonable modifications” to its services and programs, which would have included “seizure-safe housing, enhanced observation, medical review before solitary placement, alternative housing outside solitary confinement, prompt post-seizure medical evaluation, grievance access, and meaningful access to medical assistance.” (SAC ¶ 95; see also id. ¶¶ 82, 96–99 (alleging that Defendants should have provided Hart post-seizure monitoring if they had wished to place him in solitary confinement and that Defendants should have avoided placing him in the Chamber because of the loud noises).) But the complaint fails to state an ADA claim even under a failure-to- accommodate theory. Hart does not plausibly allege that Defendants were deliberately indifferent—i.e., that they (a) knew that harm to Hart’s rights was “substantially likely” and (b) failed to act upon that likelihood. See Duvall v. Cnty. of Kitsap, 260 F.3d 1124, 1138–39 (9th Cir. 2001), as amended on denial of reh’g (Oct. 11, 2001). There are no non-conclusory allegations in the complaint explaining how Defendants knew, or were supposed to know, that Hart would be seriously harmed without the accommodations identified in his complaint. Though Hart had suffered from seizures in the past and Defendants allegedly knew about Hart’s seizures, that, without more, is insufficient to give rise to a plausible inference that Defendants knew he would

metadata.case_name: Hart v. County of Mendocino

text: were supposed to know, that Hart would be seriously harmed without the accommodations identified in his complaint. Though Hart had suffered from seizures in the past and Defendants allegedly knew about Hart’s seizures, that, without more, is insufficient to give rise to a plausible inference that Defendants knew he would be seriously harmed by either being placed in solitary confinement without ongoing monitoring or being subjected to loud noises. Accordingly, the motion to dismiss this claim is granted. Dismissal is with prejudice, without leave to amend. Hart was already given an opportunity to add allegations regarding how Defendants knew he would be harmed by being put in solitary confinement or the Chamber. However, he has failed to add such allegations in the operative complaint, indicating that amendment would be futile. Deliberate Indifference Claim (Claim 2). The second amended complaint states a deliberate indifference claim against Johnston based on Hart’s allegations regarding the denial of his prescribed medication in 2024. However, the complaint fails to state a claim based on Hart’s remaining 2024 allegations and his allegations that Johnston failed to provide him medical care following a seizure in 2023. The Court discussed the 2023 allegations in its prior order. Hart alleges that after he regained consciousness following his seizure, he saw Johnston observing him with “nursing personnel.” (SAC ¶ 108.) He also alleges Johnston made the decision to withhold medical care only after verifying that Hart was “okay.” (Id. ¶ 111.) As the prior order discussed, these allegations are insufficient to support a plausible inference of deliberate indifference, see Gordon v. Cnty. of Orange, 888 F.3d 1118, 1125 (9th Cir. 2018), even given Johnston’s subsequent statement “Because I don’t care,” (SAC ¶ 113). The motion to dismiss Hart’s deliberate indifference claim stemming from his 2023 allegations is granted. On the other hand, the 2024 allegations regarding the withholding of Hart’s prescribed medication give rise to a plausible deliberate indifference claim. The complaint alleges that in July 2024, Hart was discharged from Adventist Health Ukiah Valley having been prescribed anti-seizure medication by Duncan Johnston, M.D. (Id. ¶¶ 60–61.) Defendant Eldon Johnston and other individuals allegedly denied Hart his anti-seizure medication when he requested it, which caused him pain and neurological distress, among other things. (Id. ¶¶ 116–119.) As discussed in the Court’s prior order, these allegations give rise to a plausible inference that Johnston deliberately refused to provide Hart with the

text: and other individuals allegedly denied Hart his anti-seizure medication when he requested it, which caused him pain and neurological distress, among other things. (Id. ¶¶ 116–119.) As discussed in the Court’s prior order, these allegations give rise to a plausible inference that Johnston deliberately refused to provide Hart with the medical care he needed, that such refusal was objectively unreasonable in light of Hart’s doctor’s prescription, and that Hart suffered harm as a result. See Jacobson v. Contra Costa Cnty., No. C 18-04070 WHA, 2019 WL 186649, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 14, 2019). These allegations thus state a claim for deliberate indifference against Johnston. Defendants argue that Hart’s claim is foreclosed by a “Request for Medical/Mental Health Services,” dated July 2, 2024. (Dkt. No. 1 at 64.) The Court takes judicial notice of this document, which was filed on the docket as an attachment to the original complaint. Though on the request form, Hart stated “since 7-1-24 medical refused me my meds!” (id.), that statement is not fatal to Hart’s claim. There is no indication based on the request form or otherwise that Johnston relied upon any medical opinion when allegedly refusing to provide Hart with his prescribed medication. Hart alleges that he was prescribed anti-seizure medication, that he asked multiple people including Johnston and “medical” for it, and that he ultimately did not receive it. That is sufficient at this stage. The motion is denied as to the denial of medication in 2024. The motion is granted as to Hart’s remaining 2024 allegations, including that Johnston placed Hart in the Chamber; “failed to summon appropriate care; failed to ensure medically appropriate housing; and failed to protect [Hart] from punitive isolation.” (SAC ¶ 116.) Again, these allegations do not support a plausible inference that Johston knew that his failure to take the specified actions would cause Hart serious harm. As discussed above, the mere fact that Hart had suffered seizures in the past is, without more, insufficient to support such a plausible inference. The motion is therefore granted as to these allegations. Dismissal of the claims based on the 2023 incident and the 2024 allegations other than the withholding of Hart’s anti-seizure medication is with prejudice, without leave to amend. Hart has already been given an opportunity to add allegations correcting the above deficiencies but failed to do so, which indicates that amendment would be futile. Conditions of Confinement

text: 2023 incident and the 2024 allegations other than the withholding of Hart’s anti-seizure medication is with prejudice, without leave to amend. Hart has already been given an opportunity to add allegations correcting the above deficiencies but failed to do so, which indicates that amendment would be futile. Conditions of Confinement Claim (Claim 3). The complaint fails to state conditions of confinement claims against Defendants Eldon Johnston and Jenna Johnston. As to both Hart’s allegations concerning these Defendants placing him in solitary confinement in 2023 and Eldon Johnston placing him in solitary confinement and the Chamber in 2024, the complaint fails to plausibly allege deliberate indifference for the reasons discussed above—that is, the complaint contains no non-conclusory allegations that Eldon Johnston and Jenna Johnston knew that placing Hart in solitary confinement and the Chamber would cause him serious harm. Accordingly, the motion to dismiss this claim is granted. Dismissal is with prejudice, without leave to amend, because amendment would be futile for the reasons discussed above. Procedural Due Process Claim (Claim 4). The complaint states a procedural due process claim as to Hart’s allegations concerning his placement in the Chamber but otherwise fails to state a claim based on Hart’s 2023 and 2024 placements in solitary confinement. When evaluating a procedural due process claim brought by a pretrial detainee such as Hart, a court first determines if the alleged liberty deprivation “amount[s] to punishment of the detainee” and therefore implicates the Due Process Clause. Bell v. Wolfish, 441 U.S. 520, 535 (1979). If a court concludes that the alleged deprivation amounts to punishment, it must then determine what process is due. See id. at 535–38. Absent an intent to punish, whether Defendants’ “restrictions and practices constitute punishment in the constitutional sense depends on whether they are rationally related to a legitimate nonpunitive governmental purpose and whether they appear excessive in relation to that purpose.” Id. at 561. The complaint plausibly alleges that Eldon Johnston’s decision to place Hart in the Chamber in 2024 amounted to punishment. The complaint alleges that Johnston placed Hart in the Chamber “shortly after” Hart had requested “medication and grievance forms” and that in the past Johnston had been hostile to Hart. (SAC ¶¶ 73–74.) These allegations are sufficient to support a plausible inference that Johnston placed Hart in the Chamber to punish him for requesting medication and grievance forms. (Cf. Dkt. No. 40 at 9–10.) The

metadata.case_name: Hart v. County of Mendocino

text: “medication and grievance forms” and that in the past Johnston had been hostile to Hart. (SAC ¶¶ 73–74.) These allegations are sufficient to support a plausible inference that Johnston placed Hart in the Chamber to punish him for requesting medication and grievance forms. (Cf. Dkt. No. 40 at 9–10.) The complaint also plausibly alleges that Hart’s placement in the Chamber caused him harm, including sleep deprivation, sensory overload, and neurological stress and pain. (SAC ¶ 71.) See also Demery v. Arpaio, 378 F.3d 1020, 1029 (9th Cir. 2004). The complaint therefore states a procedural due process claim arising from Hart’s allegations concerning his placement in the Chamber. The motion to dismiss is denied as to these allegations. However, Hart fails to plausibly allege that his placement in solitary confinement in 2023 and 2024 (other than his placement in the Chamber) amounted to punishment. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations that Defendants placed Hart in solitary confinement with the intention of punishing him. Furthermore, the complaint contains no allegations concerning the conditions of Hart’s solitary confinement in 2023 and 2024 (other than the Chamber). Therefore, the complaint’s allegations, which allege mere placement in solitary confinement with minimal detail regarding the conditions of that confinement, do not support a plausible inference that Hart’s confinement was excessive in relation to a legitimate nonpunitive governmental purpose, for instance, jail security. See Bell, 441 U.S. at 547 (“Prison administrators therefore should be accorded wide-ranging deference in the adoption and execution of policies and practices that in their judgment are needed to preserve internal order and discipline and to maintain institutional security.”). The motion to dismiss is granted as to these allegations. Dismissal is with prejudice, without leave to amend. Hart was given the opportunity to add allegations to his complaint concerning the conditions of his solitary confinement but failed to include such allegations in the operative complaint. (See Dkt. No. 40 at 11.) This indicates that amendment would be futile. Monell Claim (Claim 6). The second amended complaint fails to state a Monell claim against the County. The complaint contains only conclusory allegations that the County and the Sheriff’s Department had a policy and practice of, among other things, “placing medically vulnerable detainees, including detainees with epilepsy and seizure disorders, into solitary confinement, administrative segregation, or other restrictive housing without adequate medical screening, clearance, accommodation, or seizure-safe housing modification.” (SAC ¶ 160; see also id.

metadata.case_name: Hart v. County of Mendocino

text: County and the Sheriff’s Department had a policy and practice of, among other things, “placing medically vulnerable detainees, including detainees with epilepsy and seizure disorders, into solitary confinement, administrative segregation, or other restrictive housing without adequate medical screening, clearance, accommodation, or seizure-safe housing modification.” (SAC ¶ 160; see also id. ¶¶ 161–72.) Indeed, the complaint only describes events involving Hart and merely asserts that “[t]he October 2023 and July 2024 incidents were not isolated or purely discretionary acts of individual line staff. Rather, they reflected and were carried out pursuant to County-level customs, practices, training failures, supervisory failures, and ratification.” (Id. ¶ 161.) The complaint’s allegations are insufficient to support a plausible inference that the County or Sheriff’s Department had a municipal policy or custom giving rise to the events at issue in Hart’s complaint. See Hunter v. Cnty. of Sacramento, 652 F.3d 1225, 1233 (9th Cir. 2011). Accordingly, the motion to dismiss is granted as to this claim. Dismissal is with prejudice, without leave to amend. Hart was already given an opportunity to add allegations regarding the existence of a County or Sheriff’s Department policy or practice. His failure to add such allegations to the operative complaint indicates amendment would be futile. Negligence and Medical Negligence Claims (Claims 7, 8). The second amended complaint fails to state a negligence or medical negligence claim against the County. “[D]irect tort liability against a municipality must be authorized by statute.” Jones v. Cnty. of Del Norte, No. C 08-03222 CW, 2010 WL 114013, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 7, 2010) (citing Cal. Gov. Code § 815). The complaint fails to allege any statutory basis for liability. Therefore, the negligence claims against the County are dismissed. See Sowash v. Cnty. of San Mateo, No. 25-cv-09630- MMC, 2026 WL 76697, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 9, 2026). In his opposition to the motion to dismiss, Hart argues that California Government Code section 845.6 provides a basis for holding the County liable. That statute is not pled as a basis for negligence liability, as Hart has pled only common law negligence claims, and the County therefore understandably does not respond to it on the merits. Because it is not clear from the record whether amendment would be futile, dismissal is without prejudice to Hart seeking leave to amend to add such a claim via stipulation or pursuant to Rule 15. Claims Against Kendall. The second

text: therefore understandably does not respond to it on the merits. Because it is not clear from the record whether amendment would be futile, dismissal is without prejudice to Hart seeking leave to amend to add such a claim via stipulation or pursuant to Rule 15. Claims Against Kendall. The second amended complaint contains only conclusory allegations that Kendall “allowed, maintained, and/or ratified housing, classification, seizure response, and medication-continuity practices that predictably exposed epileptic detainees to unnecessary risk.” (SAC ¶ 84.) These allegations are based solely on the fact that Kendall was the “final policymaker for the Mendocino County Sheriff’s Office and Mendocino County Jail regarding jail operations, custody policies, classification practices, administrative segregation, staff training, supervision, medical-response coordination, medication-continuity procedures, grievance practices, and disability-related accommodation practices.” (Id. ¶ 156.) The complaint also alleges Kendall “knew, or reasonably should have known, that detainees with seizure disorders predictably require seizure-safe housing, timely emergency response, post- seizure medical evaluation, medication continuity, and reasonable accommodation from conditions likely to worsen seizure risk.” (Id. ¶ 158.) These allegations are insufficient to support a plausible inference that Kendall was personally involved in any alleged constitutional violations or that there was a causal connection between his conduct and any alleged violations. See Rodriguez v. Cnty. of Los Angeles, 891 F.3d 776, 798 (9th Cir. 2018) (citation omitted). Accordingly, the motion to dismiss the claims against Kendall is granted. Hart was given an opportunity to correct the deficiencies associated with his claims against Kendall but has failed to do so, indicating amendment would be futile. Therefore, dismissal is with prejudice, without leave to amend. Conclusion. For the foregoing reasons, the motion to dismiss is granted as to the ADA claim, deliberate indifference claims arising from Hart’s 2023 and 2024 allegations regarding his solitary confinement, conditions of confinement claim, procedural due process claims arising from Hart’s 2023 and 2024 solitary confinement (except as to his placement in the Chamber in 2024), Monell claim, negligence and medical negligence claims against the County, Bane Act claim, ITED claim, section 845.6 claim, and claims against Kendall. The motion is denied as to the remaining claims. The case shall therefore proceed on the following claims: the deliberate indifference and negligence claims against Eldon Johnston based on Hart’s allegations that Johnston denied him his prescribed medication in 2024, the procedural due process and First Amendment claims against Johnston based on Hart’s placement in the

text: ORDER GRANTING PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION WHYTE, District Judge. Plaintiff eBay, Inc.’s (“eBay”) motion for preliminary injunction was heard by the court on April 14, 2000. The court has read the moving and responding papers 1 and heard the argument of counsel. For the reasons set forth below, the court preliminarily enjoins defendant Bidder’s Edge, Inc. (“BE”) from accessing eBay’s computer systems by use of any automated querying program without eBay’s written authorization. I. BACKGROUND eBay is an Internet-based, person-to-person trading site. (Jordan Decl. ¶ 3.) eBay offers sellers the ability to list items for sale and prospective buyers the ability to search those listings and bid on items. (Id.) The seller can set the terms and conditions of the auction. (Id.) The item is sold -to the highest bidder. (Id.) The transaction is consummated directly between the buyer and seller without eBay’s involvement. (Id.) A potential purchaser looking for a particular item can access the eBay site and perform a key word search for relevant auctions and bidding status. (Id.) eBay has also created category listings that identify items in over 2500 categories, such as antiques, computers, and dolls. (Id.) Users may browse these category listing pages to identify items of interest. (Id.) Users of the eBay site must register and agree to the eBay User Agreement. (Id. ¶ 4.) Users agree to the seven page User Agreement by clicking on an “I Accept” button located at the end of the User Agreement. (Id. Ex. D.) The current version of the User Agreement prohibits the use of “any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy our web pages or the content contained herein without our prior expressed written permission.” (Id.) It is not clear that the version of the User Agreement in effect at the time BE began searching the eBay site prohibited such activity, or that BE ever agreed to comply with the User Agreement. eBay currently has over 7 million registered users. (Jordan Decl. ¶ 4.) Over 400,-000 new items are added to the site every day. (Id.) Every minute, 600 bids are placed on almost 3 million items. (Id.) Users currently perform, on average, 10 million searches per day on eBay’s database. Bidding for and sales of items are continuously ongoing in millions of separate auctions. (Id.) A software robot is a computer program which operates across the Internet to perform searching, copying

text: on almost 3 million items. (Id.) Users currently perform, on average, 10 million searches per day on eBay’s database. Bidding for and sales of items are continuously ongoing in millions of separate auctions. (Id.) A software robot is a computer program which operates across the Internet to perform searching, copying and retrieving functions on the web sites of others. 2 (Maynor Decl. ¶ 3; Johnson-Laird Decl. ¶ 15.) A software robot is capable of exe- *1061 rating thousands of instructions per minute, far in excess of what a human can accomplish. (Maynor Decl. ¶ 3) Robots consume the processing and storage resources of a system, making that portion of the system’s capacity unavailable to the system owner or other users. (Id.) Consumption of sufficient system resources will slow the processing of the overall system and can overload the system such that it will malfunction or “crash.” (Id.) A severe malfunction can cause a loss of data and an interruption in services. (Id.) The eBay site employs “robot exclusion headers.” (Id. ¶5.) A robot exclusion header is a message, sent to computers programmed to detect and respond to such headers, that eBay does not permit unauthorized robotic activity. (Id.) Programmers who wish to comply with the Robot Exclusion Standard design their robots to read a particular data file, “robots.txt,” and to comply with the control directives it contains. (Johnson-Laird Decl. ¶ 20.) To enable computers to communicate with each other over the Internet, each is assigned a unique Internet Protocol (“IP”) address. (Maynor Decl. ¶ 6.) When a computer requests information from another computer over the Internet, the requesting computer must offer its IP address to the responding computer in order to allow a response to be sent. (Id.) These IP addresses allow the identification of the source of incoming requests. (Id.) eBay identifies robotic activity on its site by monitoring the number of incoming requests from each particular IP address. (Id. ¶7.) Once eBay identifies an IP address believed to be involved in robotic activity, an investigation into the identity, origin and owner of the IP address may be made in order to determine if the activity is legitimate or authorized. (Id. ¶ 8.) If an investigation reveals unauthorized robotic activity, eBay may attempt to ignore (“block”) any further requests from that IP address. (Id.) Attempts to block requests from particular IP addresses are not always successful. (Jd. ¶ 9;

text: in order to determine if the activity is legitimate or authorized. (Id. ¶ 8.) If an investigation reveals unauthorized robotic activity, eBay may attempt to ignore (“block”) any further requests from that IP address. (Id.) Attempts to block requests from particular IP addresses are not always successful. (Jd. ¶ 9; Johnson-Laird Decl. ¶ 27.) Organizations often install “proxy server” software on their computers. (Johnson-Laird Decl. ¶ 12.) Proxy server software acts as a focal point for outgoing Internet requests. (Id.) Proxy servers conserve system resources by directing all outgoing and incoming data traffic through a centralized portal. (Id.) Typically, organizations limit the use of their proxy servers to local users. (Id.) However, some organizations, either as a public service or because of a failure properly to protect their proxy server through the use of a “firewall,” allow their proxy servers to be accessed by remote users. (Id. ¶ 13.) Outgoing requests from remote users can be routed through such unprotected proxy servers and appear to originate from the proxy server. (Id.) Incoming responses are then received by the proxy server and routed to the remote user. (Id.) Information requests sent through such proxy servers cannot easily be traced back to the originating IP address and can be used to circumvent attempts to block queries from the originating IP address. (Id. ¶ 14.) Blocking queries from innocent third party proxy servers is both inefficient, because it creates an endless game of hide-and-seek, and potentially counterproductive, as it runs a substantial risk of blocking requests from legitimate, desirable users who use that proxy server. (Id. ¶ 22.) BE is a company with 22 employees that was founded in 1997. (Carney Decl. ¶ 2.) The BE web site debuted in November 1998. (Id. ¶ 3.) BE does not host auctions. (Id. ¶ 2.) BE is an auction aggregation site designed to offer on-line auction buyers the ability to search for items across numerous on-line auctions without having to search each host site individually. (Id.) As of March 2000, the BE web site contained information on more that five million items being auctioned on more than one hundred auction sites. (Id. ¶ 3.) BE also provides its users with additional auction-related services and information. (Id. ¶ 2.) The *1062 information available on the BE site is contained in a database of information that BE compiles through access to various auction sites such as eBay.

text: more than one hundred auction sites. (Id. ¶ 3.) BE also provides its users with additional auction-related services and information. (Id. ¶ 2.) The *1062 information available on the BE site is contained in a database of information that BE compiles through access to various auction sites such as eBay. (Id. ¶ 4.) When a user enters a search for a particular item at BE, BE searches its database and generates a list of every item in the database responsive to the search, organized by auction closing date and time. {Id. ¶ 5.) Rather than going to each host auction site one at a time, a user who goes to BE may conduct a single search to obtain information about that item on every auction site tracked by BE. {Id. ¶ 6.) It is important to include information regarding eBay auctions on the BE site because eBay is by far the biggest consumer to consumer on-line auction site. {Id.) On June 16, 1997, over a year before the BE web site debuted, Peter Leeds 3 wrote an email in response to an email from Kimbo Mundy, co-founder of BE. (Ritchey Decl. Ex 6.) LEGAL STANDARD To obtain preliminary injunctive relief, a movant must demonstrate “either a likelihood of success on the merits and the possibility of irreparable injury, or that serious questions going to the merits were raised and the balance of hardships tips *1064 sharply in its favor.”

metadata.case_name: eBay, Inc. v. Bidder's Edge, Inc.

text: eBay site. 6 II. LEGAL STANDARD To obtain preliminary injunctive relief, a movant must demonstrate “either a likelihood of success on the merits and the possibility of irreparable injury, or that serious questions going to the merits were raised and the balance of hardships tips *1064 sharply in its favor.” Sega Enterprises Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc., F.2d 1510, (9th Cir.1992) (citations omitted). The alternatives in the above standard represent “extremes of a single continuum,” rather than two separate tests. Benda v. Grand Lodge of Int’l Ass’n of Machinists & Aerospace Workers, F.2d 308, 315 (9th Cir.1978). “The critical element in determining the test to be applied is the relative hardship to the parties. If the balance of harm tips decidedly toward the plaintiff, then the plaintiff need not show as robust a likelihood of success on the merits as when the balance tips less decidedly.” Alaska v. Native Village of Venetie, F.2d 1384, 1389 (9th Cir.1988). A “serious question” is one on which the movant has a “fair chance of success on the merits.” Sierra On-Line, Inc. v. Phoenix Software, Inc., F.2d 1415, 1421 (9th Cir.1984). Generally, the “balance of harm” evaluation should precede the “likelihood of success analysis” because until the balance of harm has been evaluated the court cannot know how strong and substantial the plaintiffs showing of the likelihood of success must be. See Village of Venetie, F.2d at 1389. III. ANALYSIS A. Balance of Harm eBay asserts that it will suffer four types of irreparable harm if preliminary injunctive relief is not granted: (1) lost capacity of its computer systems resulting from to BE’s use of automated agents; (2) damage to eBay’s reputation and goodwill caused by BE’s misleading postings; (3) dilution of the eBay mark; and (4) BE’s unjust enrichment. 7 (Mot. at 23:18-25.) The harm eBay alleges it will suffer can be divided into two categories. The first type of harm is harm that eBay alleges it will suffer as a result of BE’s automated query programs burdening eBay’s computer system (“system harm”). The second type of harm is harm that eBay alleges it will suffer as a result of BE’s misrepresentations regarding the information that BE obtains through the use of these automated query programs (“reputational harm”). As noted above, eBay does not seek an injunction that is tailored to independently address the manner in which BE uses the information it obtains from

metadata.case_name: eBay, Inc. v. Bidder's Edge, Inc.

text: will suffer as a result of BE’s misrepresentations regarding the information that BE obtains through the use of these automated query programs (“reputational harm”). As noted above, eBay does not seek an injunction that is tailored to independently address the manner in which BE uses the information it obtains from eBay. 8 Even without accessing eBay’s computer systems by robot, BE could inflict reputational harm by misrepresenting the contents of eBay’s auction database or by misusing eBay’s trademark. Moreover, allowing frequent and complete recursive searching of eBay’s database (which would presumably exacerbate the system harm), requiring appropriate disclaimers regarding the accuracy of BE’s listings, or limiting BE’s use of the eBay mark would all reduce or eliminate the possibility of reputational harm, without requiring the drastic remedy of enjoining BE from accessing eBay’s database. 9 Since eBay does not move independently or alternatively for injunctive relief tailored toward the alleged reputa-tional harm, the court does not include the alleged reputational harm in the balance of harm analysis, nor does the court address the merits of the causes of action based on the alleged reputational harm in the likelihood of success analysis. According to eBay, the load on its servers resulting from BE’s web crawlers represents between 1.11% and 1.53% of the total load on eBay’s listing servers. eBay alleges both economic loss from BE’s current activities and potential harm re *1065 suiting from the total crawling of BE and others. In alleging economic harm, eBay’s argument is that eBay has expended considerable time, effort and money to create its computer system, and that BE should have to pay for the portion of eBay’s system BE uses. eBay attributes a pro rata portion of the costs of maintaining its entire system to the BE activity. However, eBay does not indicate that these expenses are incrementally incurred because of BE’s activities, nor that any particular service disruption can be attributed to BE’s activities. 10 eBay provides no support for the proposition that the pro rata costs of obtaining an item represent the appropriate measure of damages for unauthorized use. In contrast, California law appears settled that the appropriate measure of damages is the actual harm inflicted by the conduct: Where the conduct complained of does not amount to a substantial interference with possession or the right thereto, but consists of intermeddling with or use of or damages to the personal property, the

metadata.case_name: eBay, Inc. v. Bidder's Edge, Inc.

text: law appears settled that the appropriate measure of damages is the actual harm inflicted by the conduct: Where the conduct complained of does not amount to a substantial interference with possession or the right thereto, but consists of intermeddling with or use of or damages to the personal property, the owner has a cause of action for trespass or case, and may recover only the actual damages suffered by reason of the impairment of the property or the loss of its use. Zaslow v. Kroenert, Cal.2d 541, 551, 176 P.2d 1 (1946). Moreover, even if BE is inflicting incremental maintenance costs on eBay, potentially calculable monetary damages are not generally a proper foundation for a preliminary injunction. See e.g., Sampson v. Murray, U.S. 61, 90, 94 S.Ct. 937, 39 L.Ed.2d 166 (1974). Nor does eBay appear to have made the required showing that this is the type of extraordinary case in which monetary damages may support equitable relief. Although the court suspects that the Internet will not only survive, but continue to grow and develop regardless of the outcome of this litigation, the court also recognizes that it is poorly suited to determine what balance between encouraging the exchange of information, and preserving economic incentives to create, will maximize the public good. The Ninth Circuit has noted that in evaluating whether to issue a preliminary injunction, the district court is under no obligation to consider the merits *1073 of any antitrust counterclaims once the plaintiff has demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits. There are numerous ways in which search engines can obtain information in compliance with exclusion headers, including; obtaining consent, abiding by the robot.txt file guidelines, or manually searching the sites. BE did not present any evidence of any site ever complaining about the activities of any of these search engines. 6 .The bulk of eBay’s moving papers and declarations address the alleged misuse of the eBay mark and the information BE obtains from the eBay computers. The court does not address the facts specific to these claims, nor the merits of these claims. Even if eBay were able to establish a likelihood of success on the merits as to these causes of action, such a showing would only support injunctive relief addressing BE’s use of the eBay mark and BE’s use of the eBay auction listings (the appropriate relief for which would appear to be a disclaimer regarding the lack of affiliation between eBay and BE and explicitly alerting customers to the limited scope of BE’s information). Such a showing would not be sufficient to enjoin BE from accessing eBay's computer systems, which is the only relief eBay appears to request. 7 . eBay does not appear to offer any support for the proposition that unjust enrichment is an independent cause of action, let alone an independently adequate basis for preliminary injunctive relief. 8 . Although, as a practical matter, enjoining BE from accessing eBay's computers or searching eBay’s auction database may result in BE’s inability to make effective use of information from eBay’s auction site. 9 .Thus, eBay’s motion appears to be, in part, a tactical effort to increase the strength of its license negotiating position and not just a genuine effort to prevent irreparable harm. 10 . This case was filed on December 10, 1999. BE decommissioned a number of its servers in mid-December 1999. (See Mundy Depo. at 75:12-14.) Reformatting the hard drives resulted in the destruction of the server logs that may have indicated the actual duration of access to eBay's system. (See id.

metadata.case_name: eBay, Inc. v. Bidder's Edge, Inc.

text: . This case was filed on December 10, 1999. BE decommissioned a number of its servers in mid-December 1999. (See Mundy Depo. at 75:12-14.) Reformatting the hard drives resulted in the destruction of the server logs that may have indicated the actual duration of access to eBay's system. (See id. at 74:17-24.) eBay argues this should support an adverse inference against BE because eBay is unable to correlate BE’s access to eBay’s system with service disruptions. BE responds that these actions were a result of hardware failures unrelated to the litigation. The court agrees that these actions may support an inference that the information BE destroyed was prejudicial. However, final resolution of the fact-dependent questions regarding the circumstances under which this information was destroyed requires a more complete record. Accordingly, eBay is not entitled to a conclusive presumption of harm at this juncture in the proceedings, and eBay’s motion to strike all evidence submitted by BE relating to a lack of harm is denied. 11 . The phrase "brick and mortar" is often used to designate a traditional business when contrasting it with a predominantly, or entirely, on-line business. The phrase appears to refer to the historical reliance on conducting commerce within the context of a physical space made from materials such as brick and mortar, as opposed to the modern trend toward conducting commerce in a cyberspace made from computer programs. 12 . "If 30 or 40 companies spring into existence using similar business models, what will be the total load and impact on eBay’s servers?” 13 . "One crawler may currently use 1% of eBay's resources. What if hundred of users used similar crawlers?” 14 . "Given that Bidder’s Edge can be seen to have imposed a load of 1.53% on eBay’s listing servers, simple arithmetic and economics reveal how only a few more such companies deploying rude robots [that do not respect the Robot Exclusion Standard] would be required before eBay would be brought to its knees by what would be then a debilitating load.” 15 .As discussed below, eBay has a established a strong likelihood of success on the merits of the trespass claim, and is therefore entitled to preliminary injunctive relief because it has established the possibility of irreparable harm. Accordingly, the court does not reach the issue of whether the threat of increased activity would be sufficient to support preliminary injunctive relief where the

metadata.case_name: eBay, Inc. v. Bidder's Edge, Inc.

text: success on the merits of the trespass claim, and is therefore entitled to preliminary injunctive relief because it has established the possibility of irreparable harm. Accordingly, the court does not reach the issue of whether the threat of increased activity would be sufficient to support preliminary injunctive relief where the plaintiff has not made as strong of a showing of likelihood of success on the merits. 16 . As other courts have noted, applying traditional legal principles to the Internet can be troublesome. See ImOn, Inc. v. ImaginOn, Inc., F.Supp.2d 345, 346 (S.D.N.Y.2000) ("Both parties are suppliers of 'services or products' on the Internet which, as I recognize and grapple with hereafter, is one of the most fluid, rapidly developing, and virtually daily changing areas of commerce that the law has had to focus upon and endeavor to apply established principles to.”) 17 . Because BE was expressly notified that its conduct was unauthorized, it does not matter whether BE ever agreed to a version of the eBay User Agreement that prohibited robotic activity. 18 . Plaintiff believes that it may have experienced system failures and a decrease in system performance during the times that defendant was searching its system, however, it is unable to produce any correlation between its outages and defendant’s activities. Plaintiff contends that it would likely be able to produce such a correlation but for defendant’s alleged destruction of logs that recorded the details of its robotic search activities.
